text: Nontarget analysis and ﬂuorine atom balances of transformation products from UV/sul ﬁte degradation of per ﬂuoroalkyl contaminants † Bailey B. Bowers, a Zimo Lou, b Jiang Xu, c Amila O. De Silva, d Xinhua Xu, e Gregory V. Lowry f and Ryan C. Sullivan *a Per- and poly ﬂuoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are a class of thousands of highly ﬂuorinated, anthropogenic compounds that are used in a wide variety of consumer applications. Due to their widespread use and high persistence, PFAS are ubiquitous in drinking water, which is of concern due to the threats these compounds pose to human health. Reduction via the hydrated electron is a promising technology for PFAS remediation and has been well-studied. However, since previous work rarely reports ﬂuorine atom balances and often relies on suspect screening, some transformation products are likely unaccounted for. Therefore, we performed non-target analysis using high-resolution mass spectrometry on solutions of per ﬂuorooctanesulfonate (PFOS), per ﬂuorobutanesulfonate (PFBS), per ﬂuorooctanoate (PFOA), and 2,3,3,3-tetraﬂuoro-2-(heptaﬂuoropropoxy)propanoate (GenX) that had been treated with UV/sul ﬁte to produce hydrated electrons. We determined ﬂuorine atom balances for all compounds studied, ﬁnding high ﬂuorine atom balances for PFOS and PFBS. PFOA and GenX had lower overall ﬂuorine atom balances, likely due to the production of volatile or very polar transformation products that were not measured by our methods. Transformation products identi ﬁed by our analysis were consistent with literature, with a few exceptions. Namely, shorter-chain per ﬂuorosulfonates (PFSA) and their H/F substituted counterparts were also detected from PFOS. This is an unexpected result based on literature, as no documented pathway exists for the formation of shorter-chain PFSA during UV/sul ﬁte treatment. Furthermore, the nontarget approach we employed allowed for identi ﬁcation of novel, unsaturated products from the hydrated electron treatment of per ﬂuorooctanesulfonate (PFOS) that warrant further investigation. Environmental signi cance PFAS contamination is ubiquitous and poses serious hazards to human and ecosystem health. Treatment with UV/sul te generated hydrated electrons is a well- studied, promising remediation strategy, but due to the methodology used in previous work, it is unclear if the full suite of transformation products from this process have been characterized. Since transformation products from PFAS are o en still highly uorinated, and thus persistent and toxic, it is important that we fully characterize the identities of transformation products ( via nontarget high-resolution mass spectrometry) and whether or not mass or uorine closure has been reached. Introduction Per- and poly uoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are a class of thou- sands of highly uorinated, anthropogenic compounds. 1 PFAS are unique in that they are simultaneously hydrophobic and lipophobic, which has led to their widespread usage in many applications, including nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, food packaging, personal care products, and stain- proong materials. 2,3 Many PFAS are surfactants, so they are also used in aqueous- lm forming foams for reghting purposes,4 and in micro uidic devices. 5 The per uoroalkyl moiety is extremely recalcitrant due to the high strength of carbon–uorine bonds. title: Nontarget analysis and fluorine atom balances of transformation products from UV/sulfite degradation of perfluoroalkyl contaminants

text: degradation in the environment typically yield highly persistent and still per- or poly uorinated byproducts such as per- uoroalkyl acids. Therefore, PFAS are ubiquitous, contami- nating surface water, aquifers and groundwater, as well as soil and sediment. 6 Furthermore, drinking water is sourced from surface water, aquifers, and groundwater, and conventional water treatment methods (such as occulation, coagulation, chlorination, ozonation, or other advanced oxidation processes) are not e ﬀective at removing PFAS, leading to widespread PFAS contamination of drinking water. 7,8 Drinking water is of particular concern since it can serve as a direct pathway for human exposure. A recent US EPA study measured PFAS in the source and treated waters of 25 drinking water treatment plants and detected per uorobutanesulfonate (PFBS) and peruorooctanoate (PFOA) at parts per trillion levels or higher in all samples collected. 9 Many other PFAS species were detected in at least 90% of the samples collected, further indicating the ubiquity of these compounds. 9 It has been demonstrated that frequency of detection of PFAS in water treatment plants correlates with the number of proximal mili- tary re training areas or industrial sites that manufacture or use PFAS. 10 PFAS are also ubiquitous in humans. Over 99% of National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) partici- pants age 12 and older had detectable levels of one or more PFAS in their blood serum. 11 As with drinking water, those living in close proximity to industrial sites that use or manufacture PFAS have elevated blood serum concentrations. 12,13 Human exposure to PFAS is of concern due to their association with liver toxicity, high cholesterol, bladder and other types of cancer, asthma, and fertility problems. 14 PFAS concentrations in chil- dren's blood serum have been correlated with decreased immune response to routine vaccinations. 15 Furthermore, bur- geoning evidence suggest some PFAS are endocrine disruptors, especially of the thyroid system. 16,17 Endocrine disrupting eﬀects are o en greater at lower doses, further motivating the need to remove even trace levels of PFAS from water. One promising remediation strategy for PFAS is reduction, which is a logical approach given the electronegative nature of the uorine atom. Reduction is usually achieved by UV irradi- ation of inorganic anions or organic chromophores. This yields a hydrated electron, which can reduce PFAS. It is important to note that because the uorine atom lacks d-orbitals, electrons added through reduction will be placed into high-lying energy antibonding p-orbitals, which creates a high energy barrier for reduction. Nonetheless, many per uoroalkyl carboxylic acids, some per uoroalkyl sulfonic acids, and hexa uoropropylene oxide dimer acid (GenX) can be completely degraded by the hydrated electron on the timescale of hours to days, depending on the speci c reaction conditions. 18–21 A key takeaway from previous work on hydrated electron remediation of PFAS is that the rate and mechanism both depend largely on the structure of the speci c PFAS being degraded. 18–21 Peruoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCA) such as peruorooctanoic acid (PFOA) are more readily degraded than peruoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSA), such as per- uorooctanesulfonate (PFOS) or per uorobutanesulfonate (PFBS). Other work from our group found the observed rate constant of PFOA degradation via hydrated electron was 3.4 times higher than that of PFOS and 200 times greater than that of PFBS. 22 This nding is corroborated by others, in which the rate constant of PFOA decay was 5.34 times greater than that of PFOS. 23 Furthermore, per uoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCAs) and per uoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSAs) follow di ﬀerent mechanisms of degradation. 18–21 The rst pathway for PFCA involves two H/F exchanges at the a-carbon. The resulting product is recalcitrant, since the direct linkage between the uorinated carbon and the carboxylate group is important for reduction, but subsequent H/F exchanges can occur. The second pathway for PFCA starts with decarboxylation, yielding a per uoroalcohol, which could be volatile depending on its chain length. Subsequent HF elimination yields an acyl uo- ride, which is also volatile. The acyl uoride is then rapidly hydrolyzed to yield a PFCA with one fewer carbon in its uori- nated chain. 18 PFSA, on the other hand, undergo H/F exchange in the middle of the uorinated chain, due to the higher electron- withdrawing capability of the sulfonate as compared to the carboxylate. 18 This can proceed for several cycles, until the C –F bond dissociation energy becomes prohibitively high. Alterna- tively, the sulfonate headgroup of the PFSA can dissociate, ultimately transforming the PFSA to an analogous PFCA. At this point, the PFCA pathway is taken, allowing for chain- shortening. It is worth noting the possibility for PFSA to directly undergo chain shortening via C–C cleavage, although this is likely a minor pathway since the dissociation of the sulfate is preferred thermodynamically. 20,24 The length of the uorinated carbon chain is also an important factor dictating the rate of reduction, as long-chain compounds are degraded more readily than short-chain ones. The eﬀect of chain length is especially pronounced for sulfonic acids: over 48 hours of UV/ sulte treatment, Bentel et al. observed 98% degradation of the C8 PFSA per uorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) but only 50% degradation of the C6 PFSA per uorohexanesulfonic acid (PFHxS) under the same conditions and timescale. Further- more, the C4 PFSA per uorobutanesulfonic acid (PFBS) was resistant to degradation. 18 Decreasing reactivity with chain length is especially problematic given that short-chained PFAS like PFBS have become common regrettable substitutions for long-chain legacy PFAS such as PFOS. 25 Another substitute for legacy PFOA is hexa uoropropylene oxide dimer acid (HFPO-DA). The ammonium salt of HFPO-DA is also known by its trade name, GenX. Hydrated electron remediation of GenX proceeds quite rapidly, albeit through diﬀerent pathways than PFCA or PFSA due to its ether moiety. In fact, ether cleavage is the major pathway by which GenX reacts with the hydrated electron, but H/F exchange or H/CF 3 exchange are also possible. 19,21 While the hydrated electron treatment of PFAS has been well- studied, a few knowledge gaps remain, especially regarding transformation products. First, it is rare for studies to report a mass or uorine balance. Even if the balance is not closed, it is crucial to report values, to facilitate transparency and motivate future work. text: atom balance values, their study was focused on uorotelomer carboxylic acids and uorotelomer sulfonic acids, not the more persistent per uoroalkyl substances. 26 In a study including PFCA and PFSA, Bentel et al. report that the uorine mass balance is not closed, but do not report values. 18 They attribute the lack of closure to a few possibilities, one of which being that novel products containing uorine could have been missed by their suspect screening strategy. This relates to the second knowledge gap in previous work – very few studies use a non- target approach. By only employing suspect screening lists based on previous literature, novel transformation products will not be detected. Therefore, to address these knowledge gaps, we performed non-target analysis using ultra-high performance liquid chromatography coupled to high-resolution mass spec- trometry (UPLC-HRMS) on solutions of PFOS, PFBS, PFOA, and GenX that had been treated with UV/sulte to generate hydrated electron reducing agents. NTA has been widely used in more complex environmental samples, which is not the approach taken here. 34–36 Rather, we use NTA on relatively simple, laboratory-generated samples to enable the discovery of novel products from the degradation of PFOS, as well as determine uorine balances using a nontargeted approach for all compounds studied. Experimental methods Materials Four PFAS compounds were studied and obtained as follows: heptadecauorooctanesulfonic acid potassium salt (PFOS, $98%, Sigma-Aldrich), sodium peruorooctanoate (PFOA, 97%, Alfa-Aesar), per uoro(2-methyl-3-oxahexanoic) acid (GenX, $96%, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), and nona uorobutane-1- sulfonic acid (PFBS, 97%, Sigma-Aldrich). Methanol ( $99.9%, VWR International) and ammonium acetate ( $98.0%, Supelco) were obtained for use in LC-MS mobile phases. Sodium sul te (Na2SO3, $98%) was obtained from Fisher Scienti c. Sodium hydroxide (NaOH, $98%) was obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. UV/sulte reduction For photodegradation experiments, 300 mL solutions of 5 ppm PFAS (PFOA, PFOS, PFBS, or GenX) in 20 mM sodium sul te were prepared with >18 M U water (Milli-Q, Millipore-Sigma) and adjusted to pH 10 with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Solu- tions were irradiated with UV light under anoxic conditions in a custom photoreactor for 180 minutes. The custom photo- reactor consisted of a 500 mL quartz tube, a 254 nm UV lamp (GPH212T5L/4, Heraeus Noblelight Ltd, China, 10 W), and anoxic conditions, achieved by purging nitrogen gas through the reactor. A schematic of the reactor can be found in the ESI (Fig. 1).† A water bath was used to maintain a temperature of 22 ± 2 °C. Solutions were continuously stirred during irradiation to ensure consistent conditions within the solution. Aqueous aliquots were sampled periodically into polypropylene vials to track reaction progress during UV irradiation using multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) via liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and ion chromatography (IC). At each timepoint, three 250 mL aliquots were removed – one for each analysis technique (LC-MS/MS, UPLC-HRMS, and IC) and stored in a refrigerator prior to analysis. Full details of these analysis methods can be found in the ESI (Section 1). † Matrix blanks were also prepared, containing only sul te and water. UPLC-HRMS analysis Transformation product analysis was conducted on a Thermo Scientic Vanquish ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC) system coupled to an Exactive Plus EMR Orbitrap high- resolution mass spectrometer (HRMS). Separation was achieved using an Agilent Zorbax Eclipse Plus C18 column (2.1 mm × 150 mm, 1.8 mm). Mobile phase consisted of 20 mM aqueous ammonium acetate (A) and methanol (B) at a ow rate of 0.250 mL min −1. Gradient elution was as follows: 0–1 min hold at 10% B, 1 –6 min increase to 100% B, 7 –10 min hold at 100% B, 10 – 11.5 minutes decrease to 10% B, 11.5 –14 min hold at 10% B. The rst 1.5 minutes of each chromatographic separation were diverted to waste to prevent nonvolatile salts from reaching the electrospray source and MS inlet. UPLC injection volume was 10 mL and each sample was injected once. Electrospray ionization source parameters can be found in the ESI (Section 2). † Compounds were detected in two modes: full MS scan from m/z 50–600 and all-ion fragmentation (AIF) scan from m/z 50–600. Both scan modes were performed at a mass resolution of 70 000. The Orbitrap is calibrated weekly with an external mass cali- bration using a mixture of reference compounds (Pierce Nega- tive Ion Calibration Solution, Thermo Scienti c), which maintains a sub-5 ppm mass accuracy. A nontarget data analysis approach was developed and per- formed using the mzMine 2.53 package. 27 Full details of data processing can be found in the ESI. † Briey, raw data was imported, peaks were identi ed using exact mass detection, chromatograms were built and deconvoluted, 28 isotopic peaks were grouped, then peak alignment and gap- lling was per- formed. Identication was performed using formula prediction, constraining possible formulae based on the formula of the parent PFAS compound and constraining mass accuracy to 5 ppm. Of the resulting peaks, only those that had a formula that resulted in a structure hit in PubChem, or those that had an exact mass that matched a suspect based on previous litera- ture 18,21 were considered. Furthermore, only features that increased in peak area over the course of reaction are consid- ered transformation products. Fragments from all-ion frag- mentation (AIF) scans were also used to inform identi cation. Following the PFAS-speci c con dence levels system proposed by Charbonnet et al. , the resulting transformation product identications can be classi ed as either Level 5a (PFAS suspect screening exact mass match), Level 3b (fragmentation-based candidate), or Level 2b (probable by diagnostic fragmentation evidence). 29 Fluorine atom balance We performed a uorine atom balance, as we anticipate uorine to be almost exclusively converted to the uoride ion or to a uorinated compound. While this appears straightforward, in our system, uorine is present in three diﬀerent forms, measured by three di ﬀerent instruments: uoride ions (measured by ion chromatography), uorine atoms in the parent PFAS compound (measured by LC-MS-MS), and uorine atoms in transformation products (measured by UPLC-HRMS). Therefore, each measurement needed to be converted to be directly comparable, as described below. We dene uoride recovery, h, as: h ¼ ½F/C0 /C138 t ½PFAS/C138 0½F content /C138 (1) where [F−]t is the uoride mass concentration in solution at timet (as measured via ion chromatography), [PFAS]0 is the initial mass concentration of the parent PFAS, and [F content] is the number of F atoms in one parent PFAS molecule ( e.g. 17 for PFOS). To facilitate direct comparison of peak areas from UPLC- HRMS analysis and the uoride mass concentrations from ion chromatography, a series of conversions are performed. First, the transformation product (TP) peak areas (as measured by UPLC-HRMS) are summed as follows: A t ¼ Xn i¼1 ½ðTP peak area t /C0 blank peak area Þ ðF atoms in TP formula Þ/C138 i (2) where n is the number of TPs detected. Note that the inherent assumption in this calculation is that all uorinated trans- formation products have the same electrospray ionization e ﬃ - ciency, which is a reasonable assumption for our work given their structural similarities. Furthermore, it is not possible to achieve true quantitation of transformation products without the use of authentic standards for these compounds, which we deemed too costly (in money and time) for our initial work in this eld. Therefore, we aimed for semi-quantitation and adopted an approach others have used to generate semi- quantitative results. 30 Then, the peak area of the parent PFAS compound is treated as follows: Bt = (parent PFAS peak area t)(F atoms in parent PFAS formula) (3) We convert the uoride recovery to a uoride equivalent peak area, Ct, as follows: Ct = ht[PFAS]0,UPLC-HRMS[F content] (4) Then, uorine balance is calculated as follows, where the “0” subscript refers to the initial concentration: F balance t ¼ At þ Bt þ Ct A0 þ B0 þ C0 (5) Results and discussion Degradation kinetics of PFAS Fig. 1 shows the degradation of the PFAS compounds studied (PFOS, PFOA, PFBS, and GenX) over the course of the reaction, alongside the uoride recovery level. The general trend matches previous observa- tions, where PFOA has been shown to react more readily with the hydrated electron in UV/sul te systems than PFOS. 18,23 Furthermore, due to its short chain length, PFBS has been shown to be quite recalcitrant, which we also observed. 18 As for the extent of de uorination, PFOS and PFOA had comparable uoride recoveries a er 180 minutes of reaction (81.4% and 77.8%, respectively). Fluoride recovery for GenX was 66.6%, and PFBS was 13.2%. Again, these values align with previous observations in literature. 18 A bene t of monitoring both PFAS parent compound decay and deuorination is that insight into the relative recalcitrance of the parent compound and its transformation products can be obtained.18 In the case of PFOA and PFOS, decay occurred substantially faster than de uorination, indicating that the resulting transformation products are more recalcitrant than PFOA itself. This is also true of GenX at later timepoints in the reaction (beyond approximately 30 minutes). However, at earlier timepoints of GenX treatment, decay rates were slower than deuorination rates, indicating that the parent PFAS is more recalcitrant than its transformation products. Due to the overall low decay of PFBS, no conclusions can be made about the relative recalcitrance of this compound relative to its trans- formation products. Fluorine atom balance A uorine atom balance was conducted to assess if our trans- formation product analysis achieved closure. Since uorine atoms are conserved and should largely remain in forms that can be detected via our analysis methods – as parent PFAS compound in solution, transformation products in solution, or uoride ions – we would expect to detect a constant total amount of uorine atoms throughout the reaction. Thus, we dene uorine atom balance as uorine atoms at t = 0 divided by uorine atoms at the timepoint of interest. Results are pre- sented in Table 1. This is di ﬀerent from the uoride recovery value that assesses the fraction of initial PFAS that was reduced to liberate F −(aq). For solutions of PFOS and PFBS, the uorine atom balance values were high for all samples, as expected. PFOA had consistently low uorine atom balances, while GenX had initially near-100% values that diminish over the course of the reaction. Likely reasons for these ndings are discussed below. text: products have been previously identi ed and mechanisms have been proposed to explain their formation. The majority of the detected transformation products are formed via H/F exchanges on PFOS, as described by Bentel et al. 18 Beyond H/F substitu- tion, the other major pathway for per uorinated sulfonic acids documented in literature is loss of the sulfonate group, followed by a cycle that ultimately transforms PFSA into an analogous PFCA. 18 At this point, the PFCA degradation pathway is fol- lowed, allowing for chain-shortening. Therefore, it would be expected to observe C8 and shorter per uorocarboxylic acids as transformation products from the hydrated electron remedia- tion of PFOS, but we do not observe these. 18 Our sample prep- aration and instrumental methods enabled detection of C8 and shorter PFCAs from PFOA reduction (discussed in detail later) so we can conclude this is a true, reliable result, and not indicative of a methodological failure. We also detected shorter-chain PFSA and their H/F substituted counterparts. This is a somewhat unexpected result based on literature, as no documented pathway exists for the formation of shorter-chain PFSA during UV/sul te treat- ment of PFSA. There are a few possible explanations for this nding. First, since our parent PFAS compounds were reagent grade due to the relatively large amount required for this study, some initial contamination was present. Namely, shorter chain peruorosulfonic acids (C 4F9O3S−,C 6F13O3S−, and C 7F15O3S−) were present alongside PFOS before reaction occurred. We can distinguish these compounds as contaminants since we analyzed t = 0 samples with UPLC-HRMS alongside samples from later timepoints. These short chain PFSA likely reacted with the hydrated electron to form short-chain H/F substituted compounds. A di ﬀerent explanation is required for the obser- vation of C 3HF6O3S− and C 5HF10O3S−, since C3 and C5 PFSA were not present in the initial solutions. We can unequivocally state that these two products of unknown formation mecha- nism contain sulfonate, due to the all-ion fragmentation (AIF) enabled by the Orbitrap UPLC-HRMS. For both C 3HF6O3S− and C5HF10O3S−, the AIF scan contains fragment peaks at m/z 79.9557 for SO 3 − and m/z 98.9542 for FSO 3 −. The lack of PFCA formation and the presence of these two short-chain products could indicate that C –C cleavage along the chain of PFSA is occurring preferentially over dissociation of the sulfonate. In terms of thermodynamics, dissociation of the sulfonate is favored over any other process, with a DE of approximately −130 kJ mol −1.24 However, loss of uoride (approximately −50 kJ mol −1) is observed, so it is not unreasonable that C –C cleavage would occur, especially in the middle of the uorinated chain (approximately −67 kJ mol −1).24 Proposed mechanisms for C –C cleavage in PFAS exist in the literature.20,24 First, PFOS loses one uoride ion, likely in the middle of the chain (due to the minimized C –F bond dissocia- tion energy at this position). The resulting radical anion complexes with a proton, leading to intramolecular electron transfer that breaks the C –C bond adjacent to the uoride ion that was lost. The positions at which C –F bond energy are minimized (at C3, C4, or C5) are consistent with the potential C–C cleavage products we observe, which have carbon chain lengths of 3 and 5. These products are not fully uorinated, indicating they underwent one H/F exchange a er cleavage. According to Park et al. , the other product resulting from C –C cleavage (a per uoroalkyl radical) would react with a proton, and then partition to the gas-phase. 20 This, combined with the fact that electrospray would likely not readily ionize this compound, explains why we don't observe this species in our UPLC-HRMS data. Another possible mechanism by which C 3HF6O3S− and C5HF10O3S− were formed is by sulfonation of a shortened peruoroalkyl radical. In this mechanism, the sulfonate headgroup from PFOS initially dissociates, forming an 8- carbon per uoroalkyl radical. This radical undergoes several chain-shortening cycles (hydro xylation of the radical, elimi- nation of HF, hydrolysis, decarb oxylation), eventually yielding a3o r5c a r b o np e ruoroalkyl radical. Assuming that the structure of the fully uorinated product (C8F15O3S−) contains a ring, the most likely identity is per- uoroethylcyclohexanesulfonate (PFECHS), which is used as a corrosion inhibitor and has been detected in the Great Lakes of North America. 33 It has not been previously detected from the hydrated electron remediation of PFOS. However, the literature spectrum of PFECHS contains a characteristic fragment at [M − 80] − which is absent from our spectrum (ESI Fig. 2 †).33 Furthermore, our spectrum contains a characteristic peak at m/z 79.9557, which corresponds to an SO 3 − fragment, whereas PFECHS tends to generate only an FSO 3 − fragment.29 Therefore, it is most likely that we are actually observing an unsaturated, linear structure (UPFOS). This is further supported by the presence of a peak at m/z 286.9827 in the AIF spectrum, indicating a C 5F11 − fragment, likely from the linear chain fragmenting at the double bond during ionization (ESI Fig. 2 †). Unsaturated PFSA have recently been detected in aqueous re- ghting foam (AFFF) mixtures and AFFF-impacted ground- water, but have not been previously reported from the hydrated electron remediation of PFOS. 34,35 Unsaturated PFCA have been observed from PFOA treatment with UV/sul te, but our nding of unsaturated PFSA is novel. 32 For unambiguous assignment of structure, comparison to authentic standards must be per- formed, leaving an opportunity for future work. The fully de uorinated C8 sulfonate (C 8H17O3S−) is also formed during the reaction, albeit at low concentrations (Fig. 4). This transformation product represents approximately 0.8% of the initial PFOS at maximum. Nonetheless, the presence of the fully deuorinated species in both samples is promising, since uorine is what imparts the persistent, bioaccumulative, and toxic e ﬀects to these PFAS compounds. Transformation products from reduction of PFBS PFBS is quite recalcitrant due to its short chain length, 18,20 so the transformation products make up a small fraction of the overall uorine balance (Fig. 5). Only two transformation products were detected. The major product is the result of a single H/F exchange from PFBS, and the minor product is an unsatu- rated version of PFBS that has lost two uorine atoms. Transformation products from PFOA Table 3 contains a list of PFOA transformation products while Fig. 6 shows the product distributions versus reaction time. All observed transformation products are to be expected based on literature, i.e., they are either H/F substitution products from PFOA, shorter chain PFCA, or H/F substitution products from shorter chain PFCA. However, some uorine-containing trans- formation products are not accounted for by our method, as indicated by the overall low uorine balance. Compounds that wouldn't be detected by our method include very polar or short- chain molecules (they would be lost during the high aqueous phase ush at the beginning of the LC method), gas-phase or volatile compounds (they would not be present in the liquid aliquots collected), or compounds that lack polarizable groups (as electrospray would not ionize these). The high reaction rate and speci c mechanism by which PFOA reacts with the hydrated electron gives rise to some products that are volatile and very polar, making the UV/sul te treated products of PFOA especially likely to evade our analysis methods. The primary pathway that PFOA undergoes is decarboxylation –hydroxyl- ation–elimination–hydrolysis, which involves volatile interme- diates such as per uorinated alcohols and acyl uorides. 18–21 The volatility of these intermediates increases with decreasing chain length, meaning the higher the extent of reaction, the more likely there are to be losses of uorine via volatile components. In the future, the headspace of the reaction vessels could be captured and analyzed via GC-MS to better close the uorine balance. This is exacerbated by the fact that the rst 1.5 minutes of each chromatographic run are diverted to waste – to avoid non-volatile sul te entering the ESI source of the instru- ment. It is likely that any very short chain products present would be lost during that time, and thus not detected. Transformation products from GenX Four transformation products were detected from GenX, all of which have been previously reported and thus have known pathways of formation involving H/F exchange, H/CF 3 exchange, and ether cleavage (Fig. 7, Table 4). 21 All trans- formation products observed except C 5F7H2O3 − are produced and then decay, which is consistent with literature. 19,21 C5F7H2O3 − is also noteworthy for its high mass error (84.3 ppm). We have chosen to still include this assignment in our discussion, since it is within 100 ppm of a known trans- formation product of GenX. Furthermore, we believe trans- parency and an open data culture is important in all science, but especially important for nontarget analysis. Therefore, we have decided to transparently report this observed exact mass in the event future work elucidates a better formula or structural match. At later timepoints, the uorine balance is quite low. This is likely due to the formation of volatile and/or very polar transformation products unaccounted for by our UPLC-HRMS analysis, such as tri uoroacetic acid and tri uoromethanol. 19,21 Broader implications Our work introduces two novel aspects to the well-studied eld of UV/sulte treatment of PFAS. First, by reporting the uorine atom balance, we transparently evaluate how well UPLC-HRMS analysis captures the transformation products from UV/sul te treatment of PFAS, informing future researchers in their experimental design. For PFOS and PFBS, UPLC-HRMS (or any LC-MS method, if taking a targeted approach) is likely su ﬃ - cient, as uorine balances approaching closure were obtained using this method. However, for PFOA and GenX, some amounts of volatile or highly polar transformation products were almost certainly formed (based on prior reported mecha- nisms), making UPLC-HRMS an incomplete analysis method that resulted in incomplete uorine balances. We suggest that future researchers utilize GC-HRMS to measure possible transformation products in the headspace, and possibly use a clean-up step to remove salts before UPLC-HRMS, to allow for detection of very polar transformation products. Second, by adopting a nontarget analysis approach as opposed to the typical suspect screening approach, we elucidated novel trans- formation products. While nontarget analysis has been exten- sively used to understand PFAS contamination of environmental matrices, our work is novel in the use of this approach towards the UV/sul te system. 34–36 Nontarget analysis enables a thorough characterization of transformation products formed, which is critical given the fact that transformation products can pose similar issues of persistence, bio- accumulation, and toxicity as their parent compounds. Shorter alkyl chain PFAS are generally more mobile in the environment. Therefore, even if 100% removal of the parent compound is observed, the hazard may not be completely eliminated. For PFOA and GenX, transformation products observed aligned well with literature studies that relied on suspect screening from known mechanisms. Generally, intermediate-length PFAS were formed, which appear to be more recalcitrant than their parent PFAS compounds. Future researchers will need to take this into account to maximize overall PFAS removal in a water treatment or contaminant remediation context. text: As for PFOS, novel transformation products were observed, indicating that previously published mechanisms are not complete. Further work remains in fully characterizing the mechanisms by which the novel TPs were formed, but none- theless, our tentative identi cation can inform future work in this area. Complete de uorination of PFOS was observed, albeit for a small percentage of the initial PFOS. Therefore, strategies to increase the de uorination extent of PFAS via the hydrated electron, and to address the possible recalcitrance of trans- formation products, are of interest in future work. Finally, our results for PFBS are in alignment with the liter- ature: its short per uorobutyl chain length resulted in recalci- trance to reduction, and the fraction of TPs formed was small relative to the parent compound concentration. Nonetheless, we also observe a small amount of a novel, unsaturated TP from PFBS, indicating again that previously published mechanisms are not complete.
